title: Heroes in Memory
subtitle: Tombs, cults, and why the Greeks worshipped their dead differently

narrativeBlocks.title: Not quite gods, not quite dead
narrativeBlocks.body: Greek heroes occupied a strange middle space: mortal once, but powerful after death. Their tombs became shrines — people left offerings at 'hero-shrines' for protection, healing, and local luck, long after the stories had calcified.

narrativeBlocks.title: Every city claims one
narrativeBlocks.body: City-states competed for famous heroes' bones. Athens displayed what it claimed were Theseus's bones, recovered from Skyros — a civic treasure that made the myth politically real. Sparta did the same for Orestes.

narrativeBlocks.title: The stories as ancient history
narrativeBlocks.body: The Greeks treated the hero-tales not as fairy-tales but as early history — genealogies ran back to heroes the way medieval kings traced to Troy. Thucydides opens his history with the Peloponnesian myth-cycle as backdrop.

narrativeBlocks.title: Festivals and games
narrativeBlocks.body: Hero-cult shaped real life: the Panathenaic games, funeral games, and hero-shrines kept the myths physically present. A Greek boy grew up knowing Theseus's road because his city told it in festivals.

narrativeBlocks.title: What 'myth' meant to them
narrativeBlocks.body: This is why the stories matter: they weren't fiction to the Greeks — they were a shared past that explained landscape, named seas, and justified cities. That is what your lessons have been walking through.
